claims.text: Unadjusted meta-analysis shows low-volume drinkers (1.3-24.9 g ethanol per day) have a reduced all-cause mortality risk compared to abstainers.
Unadjusted meta-analysis shows occasional drinkers (<1.3 g ethanol per day) have a reduced mortality risk compared to abstainers.
Unadjusted meta-analysis shows former drinkers have an elevated mortality risk compared to abstainers.
After adjusting for abstainer biases and study quality characteristics, low-volume alcohol consumption shows no significant reduction in mortality risk.
Analyses of higher-quality, bias-free studies fail to find a reduced mortality risk for low-volume alcohol drinkers.
Estimates of all-cause mortality risk from alcohol consumption are significantly altered by study design and quality characteristics.

evidence.description: Without adjustment, meta-analysis of all 87 included studies replicated the classic J-shaped curve, with low-volume drinkers (1.3-24.9 g ethanol per day) having reduced mortality risk (RR = 0.86, 95% CI [0.83, 0.90]).
Occasional drinkers (<1.3 g per day) had similar mortality risk (RR = 0.84, 95% CI [0.79, 0.89]).
former drinkers had elevated risk (RR = 1.22, 95% CI [1.14, 1.31]).
After adjustment for abstainer biases and quality-related study characteristics, no significant reduction in mortality risk was observed for low-volume drinkers (RR = 0.97, 95% CI [0.88, 1.07]).
Analyses of higher-quality bias-free studies also failed to find reduced mortality risk for low-volume alcohol drinkers.
Estimates of mortality risk from alcohol are significantly altered by study design and characteristics.

methodologies.name: Systematic review and meta-regression analysis
methodologies.description: Meta-regression analysis evaluating alcohol consumption and all-cause mortality while controlling for abstainer biases and quality-related study design characteristics.
conditions: Subgroup analysis of high-quality bias-free studies

limitations.text: Prior prospective studies misclassify former and occasional drinkers as abstainers, biasing the reference group toward ill health.

future_work.text: Incorporating bias-adjusted estimates into public policy and the formulation of low-risk drinking guidelines.
Future research on alcohol and health accounting for study design and abstainer biases.
